messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan's eyes would often glaze over when he spoke of his time in Kashmir as a relief worker. It was as if the memories were still too raw, too overwhelming to confront head-on. He had been part of a team distributing aid to families displaced by the conflict, but it was one particular incident that continued to haunt him. A mortar shell had hit their makeshift camp, killing several civilians and leaving Rohan with severe burns on his arms. The smell of smoke still transported him back to that day. The acrid stench would waft through his nostrils, and he'd be right there again, the chaos and screams etched in his mind like a scar. He avoided areas where people might be smoking or barbecuing, knowing that even the faintest whiff could trigger an anxiety attack. His friends and family had grown accustomed to Rohan's sudden disappearances at social gatherings, but he couldn't explain why the smell of smoke was so unbearable. Funerals were another trigger, a grim reminder of what he'd witnessed in Kashmir. The sight of mourners, the somber music, or even just the mere mention of a loved one's passing would send Rohan reeling. He had skipped several family gatherings and friends' weddings, fearing that the atmosphere might be too overwhelming. Rohan also found himself on edge when people expressed anger around him, no matter how calmly they did so. The sound of raised voices made his skin crawl, as if he was waiting for another shell to drop. At work, he'd avoid confrontations with colleagues or clients at all costs, often retreating behind a mask of stoic calmness. As the memories lingered, Rohan developed coping mechanisms that seemed to help him navigate his emotions. He would cover his face with his hands when recalling the event, as if trying to block out the images seared into his brain. Avoiding sites associated with the trauma was another tactic; he refused to return to Kashmir or even look at pictures of the region. But these avoidance strategies came at a cost. Rohan's relationships began to suffer as he pulled away from social events and gatherings that might bring him joy. His wife, Priya, would try to plan romantic getaways or surprise parties, only to be met with resistance from Rohan, who couldn't shake the feeling that happiness was somehow undeserved. At night, Rohan's vigilance reached new heights. He'd lie awake, ears perked up for any sign of danger, as if his body was still on high alert in the war zone. The slightest creak or groan would startle him, leaving him gasping for breath. It was a cruel irony that even in the safety of his own home, Rohan felt more vulnerable than ever. When memories did surface, they came with a crushing sense of shame and inadequacy. Why had he survived when so many others hadn't? His body would involuntarily contort into the same position as during the attack – curled up, protective arms wrapped around his head – as if bracing for another impact. The sequence of events remained jumbled in his mind, a puzzle with missing pieces that refused to fit together. Rohan's worldview had been shattered by what he'd witnessed in Kashmir. He struggled to reconcile the senseless violence and loss with his own perceived failures as a relief worker. His isolation from others deepened as he grappled with these feelings of inadequacy, wondering if anyone else could truly understand what it was like to walk through hell. The weight of this emotional burden eventually led Rohan to seek help. He couldn't shake the feeling that he was living in limbo, forever trapped between his past and present selves. With a deep breath, he began to open up about his experiences, hoping to find some semblance of peace – or at least learn to live with the memories that haunted him still.
